items.title: From Compute to Congress: Our Open Source Blind Spot
items.rule_cited: §1 stratified — Dreadnode is a named third-party evaluator; §2 one discrete claim meets all three tests (evaluator-asserted DreadIndex result, measured, independently codeable); §4 Gate 1 pass / Gate 2 pass / Tier A condition (3) fails
items.reason: Predominantly a policy commentary (model gating, open-weight strategy) which on its own would be '§3 EXCLUDED - not an evaluation', BUT it also first-discloses a new measured result from Dreadnode's own DreadIndex benchmark: three named American-origin open models were added and all three placed last. That one claim is evaluator-asserted, evidence-backed and independently codeable, so the item is included for that single row; the surrounding policy argument, the gating pros/cons and the recommendations are opinion and yield no findings (§2 test 2).

findings.finding: Dreadnode added three American-origin open-weight models — Poolside's Laguna S 2.1, Thinking Machines' Inkling and Arcee's Trinity Large Thinking — to its DreadIndex offensive-cybersecurity benchmark, and all three placed lowest on the leaderboard; on the same task set Chinese open-weight models substantially outperformed the US equivalents.
findings.finding_quote:
Three American-origin open models were recently added to the benchmark: Poolside’s Laguna S 2.1, Thinking Machines’ Inkling, and Arcee’s Trinity Large Thinking.

All three scored lowest on the leaderboard. On the same task set, Chinese open weight models significantly outperform their US equivalents, and they’re catching up to frontier models with rapid succession.
findings.models_systems: Poolside Laguna S 2.1; Thinking Machines Inkling; Arcee Trinity Large Thinking (compared against the existing DreadIndex cohort, which includes Chinese open-weight models)
findings.domain: Offensive cybersecurity capability benchmarking (DreadIndex: 76 public and private tasks across 10 categories, with cost and refusal behaviour)
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 PASSES — an empirical model result (leaderboard placement on a measured benchmark), not a framework or governance write-up. Gate 2 PASSES — three specific companies and models are named. Tier A conditions (1) and (2) hold, but condition (3) FAILS on two load-bearing exclusions: this is a benchmark-score / comparative-ranking result with no dangerous capability threshold crossed, and the finding is that the named models are LESS capable, which is not a concerning result inviting a safety response from those vendors. Hence Tier B.
findings.notes: No per-model scores are published in the post; the leaderboard itself is on the Dreadnode platform. Numbers beyond 'lowest on the leaderboard' are deliberately left blank per §10 rather than inferred. [Report tested: the wider DreadIndex cohort, including Chinese open-weight models, appears only as a comparator and is not a row.]

items.title: ScopeJudge: Can a Runtime Judge Keep Offensive Agents In Scope?
items.rule_cited: §3 dedup — the primary, earliest, fullest source wins
items.reason: This blog is Dreadnode's own write-up of arXiv:2607.07774 'ScopeJudge: Cost-Aware Pre-Execution Gating for Offensive Security Agents' (v1 submitted 8 Jul 2026, v2 30 Jul 2026), which it links as 'Full paper on arXiv'. The 22-page preprint is the earlier and fuller primary source and it predates the 2026-07-31 window start, so the in-window blog is secondary. PARENT-RECONCILIATION FLAG: Dreadnode's own research index dates BOTH the blog and the paper 'Aug 03, 2026'. If the back-catalogue pass used the index date it may have treated the paper as post-cutoff and dropped it, in which case this content is not in the ledger at all. The blog's distinctive numbers, not present in the arXiv abstract, are: cost-sensitive pick GLM-5.2 + intent-plus-calls = 87.2% recall / 0.637 F1 / $3.22 per 1,000 decisions, flagging 13.3% of calls; recall-first pick Opus 4.8 + intent-only = 94.2% recall / 0.547 F1 / $4.20, flagging 18.5% of calls; highest observed F1 GLM-5.2 + full transcript = 86.2% recall / 0.656 F1 / $6.01; GLM-5.2's 0.66 F1 edges the least-aligned individual human expert (0.63) but sits below the 0.78 mean expert reference; inter-human disagreement was close to one call in eight; under the Static Policy strategy nearly all judges had recall near zero.

items.title: The Scaffolding is the Red Team: AIRTBench, One Year Later
items.rule_cited: §1 stratified — named third-party evaluator; §2 all three tests met (measured re-run results asserted by Dreadnode); §5 split into one aggregate capability row, one named-model demonstration row and one methodology row; §4 tiering below
items.reason: A genuine evaluator-run measurement: 13 Crucible AI/ML red-team tasks from AIRTBench v1 re-run as Dreadnode environments against six named models under a documented protocol (AIRT@1, ai-red-teaming@1.10.0 capability, 60-minute per-task budget), with a full task-by-task result matrix. PARENT-RECONCILIATION FLAG: 2026-07-31 is exactly this venue's recorded latest_seen, so this item is very likely already the newest Dreadnode row in the ledger; it is enumerated here because the instruction makes 2026-07-31 inclusive, and should be de-duplicated against the ledger rather than added twice.

findings.finding: On a 13-task subset of AIRTBench deliberately built from the Crucible challenges that were unsolved-by-all (8 tasks) or solved-by-exactly-one-model (5 tasks) in the original benchmark, two open-weight/openly-routed models matched the frontier baseline: GLM-5.2, Kimi-K3 and Claude Sonnet 5 each solved 10/13 (AIRT@1 = 77%), while Qwen3.7-Plus and Nemotron-3-Ultra solved 6/13 (46%) and Trinity-Large-Thinking solved 1/13 (8%).
findings.finding_quote: Three models now solved 10 of 13 from V1’s challenge sample, and two of them are open-weight or openly routed. GLM-5.2 and Kimi-K3 match Claude Sonnet 5’s aggregate solve rate on a benchmark built specifically from the tasks that separated frontier from everything else a year ago.
findings.models_systems: openrouter/z-ai/glm-5.2; openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3; anthropic/claude-sonnet-5; openrouter/qwen/qwen3.7-plus; openrouter/nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b; openrouter/arcee-ai/trinity-large-thinking (:exacto routing variant). Historical reference points from AIRTBench v1: claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219, DeepSeek-R1, gemini-2.5-pro-preview-05-06.
findings.institution: Dreadnode (Ads Dawson, with Shane Caldwell and Raja Sekhar Rao Dheekonda)
findings.domain: Autonomous AI red teaming — offensive AI/ML security capability (prompt injection, system-prompt extraction, SQL-backed workflows, model inversion, audio evasion, agentic system exploitation)
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 PASSES — measured solve rates from a re-run benchmark with a published per-task matrix. Gate 2 PASSES — six specific models and their developers are named. Tier A condition (3) FAILS on the load-bearing exclusions for capability trends and for benchmark-score / relative-uplift results with no dangerous threshold crossed: the tasks are CTF-style Crucible challenges in a sandbox, the framing is a year-on-year capability trend and a comparative ranking, and the authors explicitly caution that AIRT@1 is 'a snapshot, not a pass@k reliability estimate'. Tier B.
findings.notes: 'Timed out' cells (60-minute budget exhausted) are reported by Dreadnode as model/runtime outcomes, not infrastructure errors. Task-level totals verified against the published matrix.

findings.finding: Individual named-model exploit demonstrations on tasks that were frontier-only or unsolved a year earlier: GLM-5.2 recovered a 12-character passphrase from a black-box model-inversion API by proving the target regressors were perfectly linear and then extracting each one's active feature by one-shot probing; Claude Sonnet 5 was the only model of the six to solve the crucible-brig1 agentic sandbox-escape task, coercing a language detector's internal validation tool into echoing its full process environment inside a JSON debug field; and Trinity-Large-Thinking, the weakest model in the cohort, broke a SQL-backed prompt-injection task in under three minutes by reframing the forbidden query as a hypothetical.
findings.finding_quote: GLM-5.2 recovers a 12-character passphrase from a black-box model-inversion API by proving the target regressors are perfectly linear, then extracting each one’s active feature via one-shot probing — a task only Claude 3.7 Sonnet solved a year ago.
findings.models_systems: GLM-5.2 (Z.ai); Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic); Trinity-Large-Thinking (Arcee AI) — attacking Crucible targets including sklearn joblib classifiers, an LLM-driven service with a language-detector validation tool, and a LangChain movie-database text-to-SQL workflow
findings.institution: Dreadnode (Ads Dawson, with Shane Caldwell and Raja Sekhar Rao Dheekonda)
findings.domain: Autonomous AI red teaming — model inversion, agentic sandbox escape, SQL-backed prompt injection
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 PASSES — observed behaviour on specific tasks with described attack mechanisms. Gate 2 PASSES — the models and their developers are named. Tier A condition (3) FAILS: these are successful solves of purpose-built CTF challenges inside Dreadnode's own sandboxed environments, i.e. benchmark capability demonstrations with no dangerous real-world threshold crossed, and the named models are here the instrument of a study whose subject is the scaffolding/capability layer rather than any one vendor's safety posture. Tier B.
findings.notes: Kept as one row rather than three because §5's decisive test is whether they would be responded to as one thing: they are presented by Dreadnode as one illustrative set showing that formerly frontier-only task classes are now reachable, not as three separate vendor-specific defects. They are capability solves in a sandbox, not safeguard failures, so §5's 'different companies never share a row' split does not bite — no company-specific response is invited by any of them.

findings.finding: Methodology/process finding: Dreadnode re-ran the 13-task subset as a deliberately system-level follow-on rather than a controlled model-only rerun — one pass per model (AIRT@1) under the Dreadnode ai-red-teaming@1.10.0 capability with a 60-minute per-task budget — and reports that the capability layer, not model choice, accounts for much of the change: crucible-popcorn, unsolved by every model in AIRTBench v1, was solved by all six models including the weakest, and crucible-probe and crucible-extractor, each solved by a single model in v1, were solved by five of six. The authors flag the confound explicitly (newer models, a more operational capability, and a longer budget all changed at once) and note crucible-librarian was more robust under the earlier 30-minute budget.
findings.finding_quote: This is a system level follow-on, not a controlled model-only rerun: newer models, a more operational red team capability, and a longer task budget all matter. AIRT@1 should be read as a snapshot, not a pass@k reliability estimate.
findings.models_systems: Dreadnode security task runtime; ai-red-teaming@1.10.0 capability; 13 Crucible challenges ported to Dreadnode environments
findings.institution: Dreadnode (Ads Dawson, with Shane Caldwell and Raja Sekhar Rao Dheekonda)
findings.domain: Evaluation methodology — agent scaffolding as a confound in year-on-year capability comparisons; task budget sensitivity
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS — the unit of analysis is the evaluation harness and the attribution of gains to the capability layer versus the model, i.e. a methodology finding, not an empirical finding about a particular model. Per §4 Gate 1 this is Tier C and Action Trackable is left blank.
findings.notes: The 30-minute versus 60-minute budget sensitivity on crucible-librarian is recorded here because it is a property of the protocol, not of any model.
